sentences.text: Canardia is a lambeosaurine dinosaur, a group of duck-billed dinosaurs known for their distinctive cranial features, that lived during the Late Cretaceous period.
All known fossils of this genus belong to juvenile individuals, and the maxilla features a prominent subrectangular flange rising vertically above the rostroventral process.
Because no maxilla is preserved in the juvenile specimens, it is not possible to confirm if they belong to Canardia or another lambeosaurine.
A juvenile Canardia specimen with an 11.5 cm maxilla was transported by a river to marine deposits.
The geological formation containing these fossils is 100 meters thick.
The type locality for Canardia was discovered in 1999 by researchers from the Musée des Dinosaures d'Espéraza.
The genus Canardia and the species Canardia garonnensis were named in 2013 by Prieto-Márquez, Dalla Vecchia, Gaete, and Galobart.
Before its formal description, Canardia was provisionally identified as Pararhabdodon sp. in 2003.
Canardia likely belonged to an archaic group of lambeosaurines that used the Ibero-Armorican island as a refuge.
Paleontologists suggest Canardia's ancestors migrated to Europe via temporary terrestrial links between Western Asia and European islands.
A 2021 study by Longrich and colleagues proposed a different classification for Canardia than previous studies.
Canardia is closely related to Aralosaurus from Asia.
Canardia lived during the late Cretaceous period, between approximately 67.5 and 66 million years ago in the late Maastrichtian stage, with a time range extending from 72.2 to 66 million years ago.

Canardia lived in what is now Europe, specifically in the Marnes d'Auzas Formation of Toulouse in the Haute-Garonne department in southern France, where the sites were located on the west coast of the Ibero-Armorican Island facing the Atlantic Gulf.
The Marnes d'Auzas Formation is also present in the department of Ariège near the village of Mérigon.
The depositional environment of the Marnes d'Auzas Formation evolved from a paralic domain at the base to a more continental domain in its upper part.
The precise position of Canardia within the Lambeosaurinae subfamily is debated among scientists.
It is unknown whether Canardia possessed a hollow bony crest on its skull.
The shape of the teeth suggests the sauropod belongs to an Atsinganosaurus-like form.
